findings.text: The second edict (Est 8:9-14) lets the Jews defend themselves; Mordecai goes out in royal robes and Susa rejoices (Est 8:15-16).

Est 8:17 holds two peoples under one decree: gladness and joy among the Jews, and fear among the peoples, which moved many of them to declare themselves Jews, "for fear of the Jews had fallen on them".

The main operation in Est 8:17 is fear moving people to change sides: a public declaration made "for fear". The verse gives fear as the only reason; it names no conviction and no God, and the book of Esther never names God.
findings.flag: the passage analysis at lines 49-51, which name no verse of their own

findings.text: Est 8:17 is a third outcome of dread laid on a people, beside Rahab, whose heart melted at what she heard, and Moab, whose dread sent for a curse: taking on the name of the feared, "for fear".
Est 8:17 and 9:2 are dread with no named giver, so a reading must not say God laid this fear.
Dread on a people that neither flees nor opposes: it joins the ones it fears (Est 8:17).

On the day the enemies "hoped to gain the mastery", "the reverse occurred" (Est 9:1); "No one could stand against them, for the fear of them had fallen on all peoples" (9:2); the officials helped, "for the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them" (9:3).
The main operation in Est 9:5 is not fear but acting at will ("as they pleased", the M18 word) against those who hated them; fear is in 9:2-3, and 9:2 states its effect: no one could stand.
With no one able to stand (Est 9:2), they "did as they pleased" (9:5): 9:5 is the outcome that completes the account of fear.

Ecc 12:1-7 is one figure of old age, framed by "Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come" (12:1) and ending "the dust returns to the earth ... and the spirit returns to God who gave it" (12:7).
Inside the figure: "the keepers of the house tremble, and the strong men are bent" (Ecc 12:3); "one rises up at the sound of a bird" (12:4); then the fear of high places and of the road (12:5).
The "keepers of the house" and the "strong men" are read as the body's own parts; the figure is not explained in the text.

Fear that comes as the body fails (Ecc 12:5): of high places and of the way out of doors, with the trembling of 12:3 and the startle at a bird in 12:4, set inside the call to remember the Creator before those days (12:1). It is not fear of a threat: the person is the one acted on, and the cause is age.

Psa 103:8-18 says "those who fear him" three times: the love "as high as the heavens" (103:11), the Father's compassion (103:13), and the steadfast love "from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him" (103:17).
The passage then says who they are: "those who keep his covenant and remember to do his commandments" (Psa 103:18); between these lines, "he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust" (103:14).
The main operation in Psa 103:11 is God's steadfast love toward the one who fears him: the height word (M08) is a measure, and fear is the standing of the one loved.
Psa 103:17-18 joins fear to keeping and remembering: those who fear him are "those who keep his covenant and remember to do his commandments".
